impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for method claims directed to administering a genus of antibodies requires the patentee to enable the full scope of the claimed genus, or whether enablement of representative species suffices.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding undermines medical innovation by sustaining overly broad claims and conflicts with Supreme Court enablement precedent. The decision preserves a potentially permissive enablement standard for method claims covering a broad genus of biological compounds.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method claims covering biological genera benefit from a more permissive enablement standard, potentially allowing broader patent protection for antibody-based therapeutics.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitor pharmaceutical and biotech companies face broader blocking patents on therapeutic methods, as the decision may allow patentees to claim entire genera of antibodies without enabling the full scope, raising barriers to entry for biosimilars and new drug development.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly excluded trade secret damages models and correctly assessed breach of contract damages arising from Ford's development of competing software while licensing Versata's trade secret software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously excluded damages models. The court reversed the breach of contract damages ruling and reinstated the jury award, while affirming liability for trade secret misappropriation under the DTSA and Michigan UTSA. The case involves Ford's development of replacement software while licensing Versata's automotive configuration tools.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors and trade secret owners benefit from the reinstatement of the jury's breach of contract award and the court's instruction to reconsider broader damages theories, strengthening remedies for misappropriation during licensing relationships.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop competing in-house solutions while licensing third-party software face significant misappropriation liability risk, with the court endorsing broader damages methodologies on remand.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the licensed patents such that the licensee could sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee had ceased business operations triggering automatic termination of the license.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, entitling TexasLDPC to sue in its own name without joining A&M. The court also held that TexasLDPC's shift to enforcement-only operations did not constitute cessation of business operations under the license agreement. This revives patent infringement claims involving LDPC error correction code technology used in semiconductors.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from clarification that enforcement-focused business models do not trigger termination clauses, and that exclusive licenses can convey sufficient rights to sue independently.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies accused of infringement face continued exposure to suits by exclusive licensees operating primarily as enforcement vehicles, as courts may find such entities have standing even without manufacturing or commercialization activities.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents, in a case involving communication systems using non-uniform constellations. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages. This decision provides important guidance on the Alice/Mayo eligibility framework as applied to signal processing and communications technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications technology retain viable infringement claims and damages awards where claims are tied to specific technical implementations, with certain patent claims surviving eligibility challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Electronics manufacturers like LG face continued patent infringement liability for implementing industry-standard communication technologies, and the partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty about which communications method claims survive § 101 scrutiny.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the term 'internal diameter' in patent claims relating to oil and gas wellbore float tools, and whether infringement and validity findings were supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the judgment of infringement and remanded for further proceedings in a patent dispute over wellbore casing flotation technology. The case turned on claim construction of 'internal diameter' in claims covering rupture disc assemblies used in oil and gas drilling operations. The decision requires the district court to reconsider its infringement and validity determinations under a corrected claim construction.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in the oil and gas equipment sector benefit from the vacatur, as narrower claim constructions may eliminate infringement liability for competing downhole tools.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the energy services sector face uncertainty as the remand may narrow the scope of protection for wellbore tool patents, potentially allowing competitors to design around the claims.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in finding the asserted patent claims indefinite, and whether the claims alternatively fail the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling for claims of a patent directed to wireless communications apparatus but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds. The court held that the claims, which recite transmitting signals 'over air' using a coupler with a non-magnetic core transformer, were not enabled because practicing the full scope of the claims would require undue experimentation. This case reinforces the enablement doctrine as a meaningful constraint on overly broad patent claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Electronics manufacturers like Samsung benefit from invalidation of broad wireless communications patents, reducing exposure to infringement claims from non-practicing entities.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with broadly drafted wireless technology claims face heightened invalidity risk under the enablement requirement, particularly where claims encompass physical impossibilities or require undue experimentation across their full scope.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in dismissing a patent infringement complaint without leave to amend, awarding attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285, and sanctioning plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of VDPP's patent infringement complaint against Volkswagen without leave to amend, the award of $207,543.60 in attorney fees under § 285, and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The court found that the proposed amended complaint was futile and that counsel had impliedly agreed not to amend in exchange for an extension of time. The decision underscores the consequences of pursuing meritless patent infringement claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from strong precedent supporting fee awards and counsel sanctions in exceptional cases, deterring frivolous patent litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs and their counsel face significant financial risk from fee-shifting and sanctions when pursuing patent claims that courts deem frivolous or inadequately supported, particularly where pre-suit damages are sought without adequate notice allegations.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient analysis in denying motions for Rule 11 sanctions and attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 where the patent owner pursued infringement claims after related patents were rejected under § 101 and a related patent was invalidated.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the denial of sanctions and attorney fees, holding that the district court's order lacked sufficient detail to permit meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent holder that pursued infringement claims on electronic sweepstakes technology after the PTO rejected related patent applications under § 101 and a sister court invalidated a related patent under Alice. The decision signals that district courts must carefully explain their reasoning when denying fee motions in potentially exceptional cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the Federal Circuit's insistence on meaningful analysis of fee-shifting motions, increasing the likelihood that fees will be awarded when patent holders persist with claims after repeated § 101 rejections.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who continue litigation after adverse § 101 rulings in related proceedings face heightened risk of sanctions and fee awards, as appellate courts will scrutinize denials of such motions.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board erred in finding motivation to combine prior art references where the combination would be inoperable for the purpose of one reference but operable for the purpose of the claimed invention.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the PTAB's determination that Netlist's computer memory module patents were unpatentable as obvious, holding that the relevant inquiry for motivation to combine is whether the combination is operable for the purposes of the claimed invention, not whether it is operable for the purposes of the individual prior art references. This clarifies the standard for evaluating obviousness when combining references with different design goals.
impacts.positiveImplications: Petitioners challenging patents in IPR proceedings benefit from a standard that focuses on operability for the claimed invention rather than the prior art's intended purpose, making it easier to establish motivation to combine.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent owners in the semiconductor memory space face broader obviousness challenges, as the decision lowers the bar for combining prior art references even when such combinations would defeat the original purpose of one reference.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a contract dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent settlement agreement's contingent payment clause tied to a reexamination outcome.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a dispute concerning whether T-Mobile owed a contingent payment under a patent settlement agreement, because the dispute turned on contract interpretation under state law rather than a substantial question of patent law. The court transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. This decision clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for disputes arising from patent settlement agreements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlement agreements benefit from clarity that contractual disputes over payment terms will be adjudicated by regional circuits applying state contract law, potentially yielding more predictable outcomes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to leverage patent law expertise at the Federal Circuit for settlement agreement disputes may find themselves redirected to regional circuits, losing the perceived advantage of a patent-specialized appellate court.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement case on § 101 eligibility grounds after already determining that venue is improper and dismissing on that basis.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal on both improper venue and patent ineligibility grounds, rejecting AML's argument that after dismissing for improper venue, the court lacked authority to also rule on § 101 eligibility. The patent related to e-commerce methods using a 'bridge computer.' The decision permits district courts to issue alternative holdings on patent eligibility even when venue is lacking, creating preclusive effect on patent validity.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ability to obtain eligibility rulings even when venue is improper, potentially creating issue preclusion that prevents the same patent from being asserted in a proper venue.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that a court finding improper venue will also reach the merits of eligibility challenges, effectively invalidating patents without the case proceeding to full adjudication.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether pharmaceutical patent claims directed to crystalline salt forms of cabozantinib satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that Exelixis's patents claiming crystalline cabozantinib (L)-malate salt forms have adequate written description. The decision protects Exelixis's Cabometyx® franchise through 2030, as MSN sought to enter the market with generic versions. This ruling reinforces that pharmaceutical patents covering specific crystalline polymorphs can satisfy written description requirements based on specification disclosures of preparation methods and characterization data.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders benefit from affirmation that claims to specific crystalline salt forms can satisfy written description based on detailed specification disclosures, protecting branded drug exclusivity against generic challengers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies face continued barriers to market entry where crystalline form patents are upheld, prolonging branded drug exclusivity and delaying access to lower-cost alternatives.
